passages.text: Copy of a letter to Apion, supposedly from the beloved woman. I am amazed that, after praising me for wisdom, you write to me as though I were foolish. For, wishing to persuade me into your passion, you made your examples from the myths about the gods, not afraid to blaspheme Love, the oldest of all, as you said, upon that of all gods and humans, so that you might corrupt my soul and outrage my body. For love that consists in desires is not the leader of the gods. If he desires willingly, he is his own passion and punishment, and one who willingly suffers would not be a god. But if he unwillingly loves sexual union and, passing through our souls, is carried through our bodies as through instruments into unions with intelligible beings, then whoever makes him love and carries him is greater than he is. And again, if that very one who carries him is carried by another longing, another, greater one is found who carries that one, and an endless regress of lovers results, which is impossible. Thus there is neither one who carries nor one who is carried; rather, it is the lover's own desiring passion, increased by hope and diminished by despair.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀντίγραφον ἐπιστολῆς πρὸς Ἀππίωνα ὡς παρὰ τῆς ἐρωμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: Copy of a letter to Apion, supposedly from the beloved woman
lexical_decisions.rationale: The heading and its qualification are translated as supplied. The preceding section makes the supposed female authorship part of the narrator's fabrication.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔρως γὰρ θεῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀρχηγέτης ὁ ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις
lexical_decisions.chosen: For love that consists in desires is not the leader of the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The restriction identifies the love manifested in desires. Leader can also be originator or founding source; the argument denies that this passion rules or originates the gods, without settling a separate metaphysical theory of all forms of love.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὰς τῶν νοητῶν φέρεται συνουσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: is carried ... into unions with intelligible beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied νοητῶν concerns what is apprehensible to thought, not a silently corrected reference to mortal beings. With intelligible beings takes the genitive as the partners of union; unions of intelligible beings is a material alternative that leaves their relation broader. The unusual metaphysical reference is retained without inventing physical partners.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἀπέραντον ἐπαναφορὰ τῶν ἐρώντων γίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: an endless regress of lovers results
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated appeal to a greater mover generates an unending backward sequence. Regress renders that argumentative sequence rather than suggesting a recurring cycle at one level.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων
source_issues.issue: The supplied phrase has the feminine genitive article τῆς without an identifiable expressed feminine head. The English's equally unresolved ‘upon that of all gods and humans’ is only a literal placeholder, not a claim to recover its meaning. The construction needs source-level or scholarly resolution before publication; no missing noun, clause, or printed dot gap has been invented.

passages.text: Those unwilling to master shameful desire tell lies about the gods, so that, by pointing to the gods as having done first the things they themselves do, they may escape blame. For if the so-called gods committed adulteries for the sake of having children and not sexual excess, why did they also have relations with males? ‘But,’ he says, ‘as a favor to their beloved women, they made them into constellations.’ So were there no stars before this, until heaven was adorned with stars by adulterers on the pretext of sexual excess? And how is it that the descendants of those made into constellations are punished in Hades: Atlas weighed down, Tantalus tormented by thirst, Sisyphus pushing a rock, Tityus having his entrails dug into, and Ixion rolling endlessly around a wheel? And how is it that the lovers, being gods, made those whom they defiled into constellations, without granting this favor to themselves?

lexical_decisions.rationale: The term describes unrestrained or shameless sexual conduct in this argument. The same rendering is maintained in the two occurrences rather than replacing the second by an invented account of how constellations were formed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the descendants of those made into constellations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relationship and direction of descent are retained as the speaker's claim. They are not changed to ancestors or to the constellated figures themselves to harmonize the list with other myths.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Tityus having his entrails dug into
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive suffering and the body part are retained. No animal, instrument, or additional violent detail absent from this clause is supplied.

passages.text: They were not gods, then, but veiled representations of tyrants. For a tomb of Cronus is shown in the Caucasian mountains—not in heaven but on earth—the tomb of a savage man who devoured his children. A tomb of the sexually unrestrained Zeus of myth, who likewise swallowed his daughter Metis, is also seen in Crete. There is also Pluto's tomb at the Acherusian lake, Poseidon's on Tenos, the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae, Hermes' at Hermopolis, Ares' in Thrace, Aphrodite's on Cyprus, Dionysus' at Thebes, and those of others in other places. In any case, the tombs of the very gods mentioned are visible. For they were humans, and wicked ones and sorcerers at that. They could not otherwise have become absolute rulers—I mean the Zeus of myth and Dionysus—unless through transformation they gained control over whomever they wished for whatever purpose they themselves wished.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes enigmatic or figurative representations. The claim identifies the mythic gods as disguised presentations of human tyrants, not merely difficult riddles that tyrants posed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἡλίου δὲ ἐν Ἄτροις καὶ Σελήνης ἐν Κάρραις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae
lexical_decisions.rationale: The divine names are rendered by their transparent celestial meanings; Helios and Selene are conventional name alternatives. Atroi follows the supplied place-name spelling without silently identifying it with another city.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μὴ τῇ μεταμορφώσει ὧν ἤθελον ἐπεκράτουν εἰς ὅπερ αὐτοὶ ἤθελον
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless through transformation they gained control over whomever they wished for whatever purpose they themselves wished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive after gained control is read as those controlled, and the final phrase as the intended end. The wording does not specify whether the transformation is their own or that of others, nor explain an otherwise unnamed magical mechanism.

passages.text: If we must emulate their lives, let us imitate not only their adulteries but also their tables. For Cronus swallowed his own children, and Zeus likewise his own daughter. And what need is there to say more? Pelops became a dinner for all the gods. So let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a similar dinner to the gods'. Then the dinner would be worthy of the marriages. But you would never bear to do this, just as I would never bear to commit adultery. Besides all this, you threaten me with the wrath of Love as though he were a powerful god. Love is not a god such as he is thought to be, but a desire arising from the constitution of the living being for the succession of life, according to the providence of the one who brought everything into being. This is so that the whole race may never fail, but, on the pretext of pleasure, another may again come into being from the substance of the one who is going to die, sprung from a lawful marriage, so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age. Those born from adultery would not be able to do this, lacking a natural affection toward those who begot them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And what need is there to say more?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rhetorical question concerns what needs saying, not what one is able to say. More is supplied from the movement toward the final example, rather than changing the question into an appeal to ability.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from the constitution of the living being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun refers to the mixture or constitution of the organism. Animal is another literal rendering of ζῷον, but living being preserves its applicability to humans in this explanation.

The same pretext language used in the polemic is retained in the positive account of generation. For the sake of pleasure would flatten the distinction between the reproductive purpose and the pleasure that provides its occasion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως πρὸς τὸ γηροτροφεῖν τὸν αὐτοῦ πατέρα γνώσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age
lexical_decisions.rationale: The child is the inferred subject of knowing, with the father its expressed object and support in old age the purpose. The source's ensuing assertion about children born from adultery is retained as the fictional letter writer's claim, not presented as an established psychological fact.

passages.text: Since, then, erotic desire arises for the sake of succession and legitimate increase, as I said, parents should take thought for chastity and educate their children in advance, before desire arises, through books that teach self-restraint. They should accustom them beforehand to better teachings, because habit is a second nature. In addition, they should frequently remind them of the punishments imposed by the laws, so that, using fear like a bridle, they do not rush along with improper pleasures. It is also fitting to satisfy through marriage the natural passion of their age before desire reaches its height, having first persuaded them not to fix their eyes on the figure of a courtesan.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective concerns legitimate descent in the contrast with adultery. Genuine growth is a more literal lexical alternative, but would obscure the explicitly marital context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σωφροσύνης προνοουμένους, τοὺς αὐτῶν παῖδας πρὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας διὰ τῶν σωφρονιζόντων βιβλίων
lexical_decisions.chosen: take thought for chastity ... through books that teach self-restraint
lexical_decisions.rationale: The shared word-family concerns restraint, here especially sexual chastity. The English varies the cognate forms for natural readability while disclosing their connection; books that teach chastity is a narrower alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸ τοῦ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἐπακμάσαι γάμῳ τὸ φυσικὸν τῆς ἡλικίας πληροφορεῖν πάθος
lexical_decisions.chosen: satisfy through marriage the natural passion of their age before desire reaches its height
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ancient recommendation and its timing are retained without turning them into present-day guidance or adding an age not stated in the source. The verb denotes filling or satisfying the passion, not merely recognizing it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς εἶδος ἑταίρας γυναικὸς μὴ ἀτενίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not to fix their eyes on the figure of a courtesan
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἑταίρας is read as the noun courtesan, not silently changed to ἑτέρας, another. Figure renders visible form or appearance without adding the adjective beautiful.
